newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa commuter rail plans privatisation project.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa commuter rail plans privatisation project.

text.p: The South African Rail Commuter Corporation (SARCC) is considering a pilot project to test how privatisation could help cut the 1.3 billion rand a year commuter rail subsidy paid by the state.
Managing director Wynand Burger told the parliamentary public accounts committee on Wednesday that the SARCC and trade unions were discussing a system of "concessioning".
This was based on the concept that "you entrust your resources to somebody else, to a private operator in particular, to manage and maintain it on a very strict, predetermined, deliverable basis".
He said concessions would be introduced slowly to minimise possible labour action because of job losses.
"We are investigating the possibility in consultation with the unions," he said.
While countries such as Argentina had done this through the total privatisation of rail commuter networks, circumstances in South Africa were different and called for a more cautious approach.

"I foresee that in the medium and short term we will be looking at a negotiated concession with the current operator (Metrorail) for a number of years to allow them to practice and become conversant with the terms of that kind of agreement," Burger said.
"After a number of years one can then consider, especially with the devolution of powers to the regions, going for a more open kind of tender concession."
He said that although capital expenditure on the commuter railway service had been neglected until recently, it was still considered one of the best in the world.

"But we are lacking in service quality and cleanliness...and that is where a dedicated, small-is-beautiful approach does work and that is where the big benefits can be received from concessions," he said.

Burger said a better-run commuter rail service would help reduce costs and the subsidy needed from the state. It would also cut down on fare evasion which was currently estimated at 30 percent of potential revenue, or about 170 million rand a year.
